origin: England, Somerset (likely Kingstone near Taunton), early 1800s
harvest_window: late Sep-early Oct (WSU Mt Vernon bloom 5/12, harvest 9/30); mid-late Oct in England
disease_notes: Susceptible to apple scab and canker; notoriously erratic, low-yielding cropper that fell out of commercial UK use for this reason. WSU rates productivity only 2.7/5, among the lowest in their trial. Spreading habit, standard bearing.
description: The most celebrated English vintage-quality cider apple, emerged in Somerset in the early 1800s and possibly an open-pollinated seedling of Cap of Liberty. Cidermakers prize it as one of the very few varieties carrying enough tannin and acid together to make a complete single-varietal cider. Important local caveat: WSU-grown fruit measured only 0.15% tannin and classed as Sharp, so in this climate plan to blend it with a true bittersweet for structure.
discrepancies: Class: LARS/UK sources call it bittersharp, but WSU measured 0.15% tannin and classes it Sharp - recommended SH per WSU as climate-local; treat as a mild bittersharp at best here. Bloom: pomiferous group E (mid-late, ~4) vs WSU bloom 5/12 - recommended 3 per WSU. Acid: WSU 0.61% (medium) vs MSU Montana 0.94% (high) - recommended medium per WSU marine-climate data.

origin: USA, Essex County (South Orange/Newark), New Jersey; recorded as early as 1712, dominant 1800s
harvest_window: early-mid Oct (WSU Mt Vernon bloom 5/16, harvest 10/9)
disease_notes: Reported good resistance to fireblight, apple scab, cedar-apple rust and powdery mildew - an unusually clean tree, which matters on wet maritime sites. Upright, tip-bearing habit, so avoid heavy heading cuts. Excellent juice yield at 221 mL/lb.
description: The legendary apple of Newark cider, described by William Coxe as the most celebrated of the cider apples of Newark in New Jersey, and traditionally blended with Campfield and Granniwinkle. Believed extinct until rediscovered at an old Livingston, NJ cider mill in 1976, it is now central to the American heritage-cider revival. Cidermakers use it for an exceptionally dark, rich cider with heavy mouthfeel, and its disease resistance makes it one of the safer heritage picks for the Olympic Peninsula.
discrepancies: Class: nursery catalogs (Albemarle, Raintree) label it bittersweet, but WSU measured tannin 0.10% / acid 0.64% and classes it Sharp - recommended SH per WSU. Acid: WSU 0.64% vs MSU Montana 1.26% - recommended medium per WSU as climate-local. Biennial tendency was unknown from nursery sources; WSU records semi-alternate bearing - recommended moderate. Ploidy remains unresolved across every source checked.

origin: England, farm of Mr. Dent at Yarkhill, Herefordshire, c.1850
harvest_window: mid-late Oct (WSU Mt Vernon bloom 5/22, harvest 10/18 - the latest of this set)
disease_notes: Susceptible to apple scab and fireblight. Upright/semi-spreading spur bearer prone to limb splitting under heavy crop - benefits from support or training. Very low blind wood (1.0) and good juice yield (281 mL/lb).
description: A chance Herefordshire seedling found around 1850 and popularized by the H.P. Bulmer cider company, named for the large russet patch at the calyx end. It gives a dark cider with soft tannins and nutty, butterscotch notes, and is valued as a dependable tannin contributor in blends. Its very late bloom (latest in this group) makes it a strong frost-avoidance choice, and it is one of the few cider varieties proven suitable for mechanical harvest; the fruit does not store and should be pressed soon after picking.
discrepancies: Biennial: nursery sources (Trees of Antiquity, Roots to Fruits) call it a heavy biennial producer, but WSU records only semi-alternate bearing - recommended moderate per WSU. Class: WSU classes it Bittersweet even though its measured tannin (0.16%) sits below the 0.20% LARS bitter threshold; kept BSW per WSU's own assignment, but expect softer tannin than English-grown fruit. Bloom (late) and late harvest agree across all sources.

origin: England, Rodney Stoke / Wedmore area, Somerset; popularized 1920s
harvest_window: late Sep-early Oct (WSU Mt Vernon bloom 5/19, harvest 9/30); late Oct-Nov in England
typical_sg: 1.045 (11.7 Brix, WSU Mt Vernon - the lowest sugar of this set)
disease_notes: Highly resistant - possibly immune - to apple scab, hence the synonym Neverblight; broadly pest and disease tolerant and will tolerate shade. Susceptible to fireblight. Slow to bear (6-8 years) and twiggy, needing substantial pruning. Highest juice yield in this set at 286 mL/lb.
description: A Somerset heirloom producing vintage-quality bittersharp juice with a near-perfect tannin/acid balance, one of the short list of varieties usable as a single-varietal. WSU measured the highest tannin of any variety in this group (0.28%), so it is the most reliable structure contributor here despite its low sugar. Its outstanding scab resistance and shade tolerance make it arguably the best-suited bittersharp for a wet maritime site like the Olympic Peninsula, and its late bloom makes it a useful pollenizer for Brown Snout and Dabinett.
discrepancies: Harvest: UK sources say late Oct-Nov and that it needs a cold chill to ripen, but WSU Mt Vernon harvests 9/30 - recommended late Sep-early Oct per WSU as climate-local. Bloom: pomiferous group G (latest, ~5) vs WSU bloom 5/19 - recommended 4 per WSU. Tannin: pomiferous lists 4.3%, which is implausible as percent tannic acid and was discarded in favor of WSU's 0.28%. Biennial: WSU records alternate bearing Yes, upgrading an earlier moderate call to high.

origin: England, Colnbrook, Buckinghamshire, c.1825 (raised by Richard Cox); likely a Ribston Pippin seedling
harvest_window: mid Sep-mid Oct, typically the last week of September (northern climates)
disease_notes: Very susceptible to apple scab, powdery mildew and canker, plus fruit cracking, brown rot and papery bark. WSU Extension specifically advises scab-resistant cultivars for western Washington sites receiving 50+ inches of rain, which makes Cox a poor structural fit for this orchard without a committed spray program.
description: The benchmark English dessert apple, introduced in 1825 and ancestor of a large share of modern aromatic cultivars. Cidermakers use it for aroma rather than structure - its pear-drop and spice character survives fermentation and lifts an otherwise flat blend - but it contributes almost no tannin. Its heavy disease susceptibility in cool wet conditions is the main argument against planting it in maritime Washington.
discrepancies: Absent from WSU's 77-cultivar cider database, so there is no climate-local trial data - all values come from UK and general sources, which is why confidence is medium and typical_sg is left null. Bloom group: Cummins lists 2, Orange Pippin and the UK standard list 3 - recommended 3 as the more widely corroborated. Parentage is disputed (Ribston Pippin x possibly Blenheim Orange vs Margil x Rosemary Russet) and was left out of the record as unconfirmed.

origin: USA, Virginia; known by the mid-1700s. A Malus domestica x M. angustifolia (southern crab) hybrid
harvest_window: late Aug-early Sep (WSU Mt Vernon bloom 4/19, harvest 8/31) - the earliest harvest of this set
typical_sg: 1.060 (14.8 Brix, WSU Mt Vernon); 21 Brix / ~1.089 in drier Montana trials
disease_notes: Generally healthy and extremely cold hardy - historically used as a rootstock as far north as Maine. Susceptible to fireblight; light cedar-apple rust reported. WSU records the cleanest blind-wood rating in this set (1.0) and no alternate bearing. Fruit is tiny at 1.55 inches, so expect slow hand-harvest.
description: America's most historically important cider crab, grown by Jefferson at Monticello and the backbone of colonial Virginia cider. The fruit is tiny and fibrous but yields a viscous, high-acid juice that ferments to a structured, aromatic cider, and it is one of the few crabs capable of standing alone as a varietal. Its very early bloom plus abundant long-lasting pollen make it a valuable orchard pollenizer - but note it blooms far too early to serve the late bittersweets.
discrepancies: Tannin: MSU Montana measured 0.52% but WSU Mt Vernon measured 0.19% - recommended medium per WSU as climate-local; the Montana figure would imply markedly more bitterness than PNW-grown fruit delivers. Harvest: WSU records 8/31, well ahead of the Sep-Oct cited by East-coast sources and MSU's 9/7-9/18 - recommended late Aug-early Sep per WSU. Bloom: nurseries say early midseason, group 2, but WSU's 4/19 is the earliest date in the database - recommended 1. Biennial: nurseries say it needs thinning to hold annual bearing, WSU records no alternate bearing - recommended low per WSU.

origin: USA, East Bloomfield, New York; seedling grown c.1800 from Connecticut seed, disseminated from the Chapin farm in the 1840s
harvest_window: late Oct and beyond (one of the latest-harvested American varieties)
disease_notes: Susceptible to apple scab, most major apple diseases and bitter pit; only slightly resistant to fireblight. Immune to woolly apple aphid - the trait that made it the breeding parent of the Malling-Merton (MM.106/MM.111) rootstock series. Notoriously slow to bear: about 4 years on dwarfing stock, up to 10 on standard. Upright tip bearer with long gangly branches.
description: A famous New York heirloom, the classic American pie apple, and a very late sharp that cidermakers use as a high-acid aromatic backbone against low-acid English bittersweets. It brings bright acidity and distinctive aroma but almost no tannin, so it needs a bittersweet or crab partner for structure. It overcrops once established, so thinning is required to avoid locking in biennial bearing.
discrepancies: Absent from WSU's cider cultivar database, so no climate-local bloom, harvest or juice data - typical_sg left null rather than estimated. Bloom group: sources split between 4 and 5, both described as late - recommended 4 as the more commonly cited. Origin date varies by source (seedling grown c.1800 vs first fruiting and naming in the 1840s); both are recorded rather than picking one, since they describe different events.

origin: France, Normandy, near the commune of Bernay (Eure); 1700s
harvest_window: mid Oct (WSU Mt Vernon bloom 5/8, harvest 10/16); stores roughly one month
disease_notes: No disease-susceptibility data found in any authoritative source - treat as unknown and observe locally. WSU records a semi-spur, semi-upright habit with good productivity (3.7/5) and no alternate bearing.
description: A Normandy heirloom bittersweet said to trace to the Benedictine abbey town of Bernay, inedible fresh but long valued for cider. The greenish flesh gives a robust golden juice with a distinctive dry, smoky finish and prominent fruit character, typically used at up to about 30% of a blend, and the hard fruit grinds easily with good juice yield. WSU's marine-climate data shows it as a mid-blooming, mid-October, annually-bearing tree with moderate rather than heavy tannin.
discrepancies: Biennial: Cummins and Albemarle say it tends to biennialism while Trees of Antiquity calls it an annual heavy producer; WSU records no alternate bearing - recommended low per WSU, which breaks the tie. Tannin: nursery copy describes it as high-tannin and bitter/astringent, but WSU measured 0.19% - recommended medium per WSU. Bloom: Trees of Antiquity says late bloom, WSU's 5/8 is mid-season - recommended 3 per WSU. Ploidy unresolved in all sources; confidence raised from low to medium once WSU trial data was found.

origin: England, Yarlington, North Cadbury, Somerset; late 1700s-1800s, found as a wild seedling at a water mill and propagated by nurseryman Harry Masters
harvest_window: late Sep (WSU Mt Vernon bloom 5/13, harvest 9/26); late Oct-Nov in England
disease_notes: Some scab susceptibility; resistant to powdery mildew and canker; highly susceptible to fireblight. Slow to come into bearing, and fruit drops as soon as it ripens, so plan for prompt or windfall collection. WSU rates productivity 3.7/5 with a spreading habit and large fruit (2.74 in).
description: A Somerset chance seedling that became probably the most widely planted bittersweet cider apple worldwide, classed as a medium bittersweet under Long Ashton. It gives a traditional amber English cider with rich apple flavor, soft tannins and slight bitterness, and it is one of the few genuinely late varieties with low enough acidity to serve as a blend base. In WSU trials it carried the highest tannin of the bittersweets tested but the lowest sugar, so expect modest ABV from PNW fruit and blend for gravity.
discrepancies: Biennial: this is the largest conflict in the set - every English and nursery source describes a strong biennial tendency, but WSU Mt Vernon recorded no alternate bearing across 2002-2017. Recommended low per WSU as climate-local, though it warrants local observation before relying on it. Bloom: pomiferous puts it in group C (mid) while US nurseries call it late; WSU's 5/13 splits the difference - recommended 4. Harvest: UK sources say very late (Oct-Nov) vs WSU 9/26 - recommended late Sep per WSU.

origin: USA, orchard of Mr. Brathwaite near Bentonville, Benton County, Arkansas; c.1870, first fruited 1879. Likely a Winesap seedling
harvest_window: Oct-Nov (very late; roughly 150 days after bloom, picked over 3-4 weeks)
disease_notes: Strong resistance to powdery mildew and fireblight, moderate resistance to canker and cedar-apple rust, but susceptible to apple scab. Critical planting caveat: as a triploid it produces sterile pollen and cannot pollinate anything, so it needs two compatible diploid pollenizers with overlapping bloom.
description: A famous late-season Arkansas keeper and one of the darkest apples grown, turning nearly black on the sun side as it ripens. Its hard, fine-grained flesh is too tart at harvest and needs roughly 90 days of storage to mellow into aromatic sweetness, holding firm texture for months. Cidermakers use it as a firm, aromatic late sharp/dessert component rather than a tannin source, and the pollen sterility is the main orchard-design constraint.
discrepancies: Absent from WSU's cider cultivar database, so no climate-local data and typical_sg left null. Ploidy: pomiferous and multiple pollination charts state triploid with sterile pollen, while some nursery listings describe it as diploid - recommended triploid because the triploid claim is specific, repeated and consequential, but verify locally before counting it as a pollenizer. Long Ashton class has never been established for this variety, so it is recorded as dessert rather than forced into a cider class.

origin: USA, New York, first half of the 1800s (possibly derived from English Russet stock; origin debated)
harvest_window: early Oct (WSU Mt Vernon bloom 4/19, harvest 10/3)
typical_sg: 1.061 (15.4 Brix, WSU Mt Vernon); up to 18.2 Brix / ~1.075 in drier Montana trials
disease_notes: Resistant to apple scab and cedar-apple rust - a significant advantage in the wet maritime PNW - but susceptible to fireblight. Tip-bearing habit with long willowy branches, so avoid heavy heading cuts. Not self-fertile. WSU rates it best-in-set for bloom density (4.7/5) and productivity (3.9/5) with the largest fruit (2.83 in).
description: Widely called the champagne of cider apples and the most highly regarded North American cider variety, a bronze-russeted New York heirloom from the early 1800s. Cidermakers use it for exceptional sugar - typically the highest-gravity juice in a mixed planting, giving body and natural alcohol without chaptalization - combined with balanced acid and a nutty, honeyed depth. Its scab resistance, reliable annual cropping and top WSU productivity ratings make it one of the easiest high-value cider varieties to grow on the Olympic Peninsula.
discrepancies: Bloom: nurseries describe it as early-to-midseason (~2), but WSU records 4/19, tied for the earliest bloom in its 77-cultivar database - recommended 1 per WSU. This matters practically, since it means Golden Russet will not overlap the late bittersweets (Brown Snout, Stoke Red) and needs an early-blooming pollen partner such as Hewes Crab. Sugar: WSU 15.4 Brix / SG 1.061 vs MSU Montana 18.2 Brix / ~1.075 - recommended the WSU figure for planning here, as the drier Montana site concentrates sugar. Origin (New York vs derivation from an English russet) is disputed in the literature and left as such.
